svg.font-family: Inter, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: Figure 1. Three kinds of audit, and what each one can establish
svg.desc: Three different things are all called a VPN audit. An application security review examines the client software for vulnerabilities and says nothing about servers or logging. An infrastructure review examines server configuration and hardening. A no logging assurance engagement examines whether the system configuration is capable of retaining the data the provider says it does not retain. A band below gives four questions to ask of any audit report: its date, who commissioned it, what was in and out of scope, and whether the full report is published or only a summary. A final band explains that a no logging engagement is a point in time observation of configuration rather than a proof of behaviour over time, which is why frequency matters more than any single report.
svg.text: Figure 1: Three Different Things Are All Called "Audited"
Guidance says to check for an audit and stops there. Which audit, of what, by whom, and when, are the whole of the information.

g.text: What it examines
The client applications: memory handling,
how keys are stored, whether the kill switch
actually holds, leak behaviour.
What it establishes
That the thing on your machine was reviewed
by somebody competent at a point in time.
What it says about logging
Nothing whatsoever.

svg.text: the servers and how they are run

g.text: What it examines
Server build and hardening, how machines are
provisioned and wiped, access control, whether
storage is used at all.
What it establishes
That the estate was configured as described,
on the machines the auditor was shown.
The limit worth naming
An auditor sees the estate presented to them.

svg.text: the claim people actually care about

g.text: What it examines
Whether the system as configured is capable of
retaining the data the provider says it does
not retain. Usually under a formal standard.
What it establishes
That on the day the auditor looked, the
configuration matched the claim.
What it does not establish
What happens on a day nobody is looking.

svg.text: Four questions to ask of any audit report, in the order that matters

g.text: Which of the three is it? An application review presented as evidence of no logging is a category error, and it is the most common one in comparison articles.
What date? Infrastructure changes constantly. A report from four years ago describes a company that no longer exists in that configuration.
Who commissioned it, and what was excluded? Almost all of these are paid for by the subject, which is normal and not disqualifying.
The exclusions are stated plainly by careful auditors, and they are the most useful paragraph in the document.
Is the full report published, or a summary? A press release describing an audit is not an audit. If you cannot read the scope section, you do not know what was tested.

svg.text: And the structural limit, which no amount of auditing removes
A no logging engagement observes a configuration. It cannot observe intent, it cannot observe what happens after the auditor leaves, and it cannot detect a change made
the following week. That is not a criticism of the auditors, who are usually careful to say so themselves in the report you were not shown.
Which is why repetition matters more than any single report. Six engagements over seven years says something a first audit cannot, and an unannounced one says more again.
So "audited" on a comparison chart is not a fact about a provider. It is a prompt to go and read something.
Twenty minutes with the actual report tells you more than any number of articles about it.
